Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAP View image in fullscreen Temperatures in Sydney during the first days of September are on track to match the city’s midsummer average of 26.4C. Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAP Australia weather Sydney set to hit 33C in warmest start to spring since mid-1800s, while snow forecast in southern NSW A total fire ban is in place for greater Sydney with extreme fire danger exacerbated by hot and windy conditions Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australian Associated Press with Guardian staff Fri 4 Sep 2026 22.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 22.07 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Summer heat is due to arrive early across much of eastern Australia with potentially record early September temperatures predicted for Brisbane and Sydney, while snow was expected in southern New South Wales . Maximum temperatures in Sydney during the first days of September were on track to match the city’s midsummer average of 26.4C, warmer than any other start to spring since the city’s Observatory Hill station opened in 1858. Suburbs across Sydney were expected to reach up to 33C on Saturday afternoon, smashing average September records by up to 13C. BoM forecasts strongest El Niño on record as research points to ‘alarming’ climate change influence Read more The meteorologist Tom Saunders said a gusty north-westerly airstream blowing south from the northern interior would lift maximums this weekend by as much as 13C above the average. The highest anomalies were set to impact the NSW coast. “For Sydney, it’s likely to be the hottest day this early in spring on record and for the first five days of September we’re on track to average a top of 27 degrees that matches the midsummer average,” he told ABC News. “Temperatures this spring will average as much as three degrees above the baseline from recent decades, potentially the hottest spring on record.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The warm, dry and windy conditions would cause fire dangers to spike. A total fire ban was in place for the greater Sydney region, where extreme fire danger was forecast. The dramatic – and potentially dangerous – start to Australia’s spring extended across much of the continent, with damaging winds that could bring down trees and roofs in South Australia , and minor to moderate flooding for parts of Victoria and Tasmania. Meanwhile, in southern NSW, snow was on late Saturday morning falling in Thredbo in the Snowy Mountains. The Bureau of Meteorology had forecast snowfall to hit Thredbo top station by 4pm on Saturday, with a daytime low temperature of -1C. The new falls won’t do much to help the parlous cover remaining on Australia’s ski fields after a warm winter, however. The Weatherzone journalist Anthony Sharwood on Friday wrote: “September snowfalls are meaningful when there’s a decent remnant snowpack from winter onto which the new snow can bond. But … the Australian snowpack is at a historic low for the first week of September, even at the highest elevations of the mountains.” Across the border, southern Queensland would see temperatures peak in the mid-30s in another unseasonably warm start to September. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion In South Australia’s Mount Lofty and Flinders ranges, wind gusts of up to 110kmh were possible late Saturday into Sunday morning. Heavy rains were forecast for north-east Victoria and northern Tasmania, with up to 60mm expected in some parts. “The catchments in those areas are really wet,” the BoM meteorologist David Crock said on Friday. “They’ve seen multiple rounds of flood warnings this winter already. “So we’ve got a flood watch current again for these catchments across northern Victoria … and across parts of northern Tasmania as well.” The dramatic start to spring comes against the background of a “supersized” El Niño weather phenomenon to Australia’s east, one that is already breaking heat records, and could comfortably surpass previous events. On Thursday, the UN’s weather agency said the event in the Pacific was continuing to strengthen and would probably persist until early 2027, warning it had the “potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world”. El Niño events tend to mean hotter and drier conditions for Australia’s south and east in winter and spring, and can increase the risk of heatwaves, drought and bushfires. Australia’s national council for fire and emergency services said fire authorities were predicting a heightened risk of fire across northern and south-eastern NSW, south-east Queensland, north-eastern Tasmania, parts of Western Australia, South Australia and Victoria, and large parts of the Northern Territory. Photograph: David Swanson/AFP/Getty Images Weather tracker Extreme weather Analysis Weather tracker: Floods in eastern India and hurricane damage in California Magdalena Shopova for MetDesk Flooding in West Bengal has led to three deaths, while severe beach erosion has been witnessed in Orange county Mon 14 Sep 2026 05.28 EDT Last modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 05.40 EDT Share Flooding around the city of Malda in the Indian state of West Bengal since Thursday has had a devastating effect. So far, three deaths have been recorded and many areas are still flooded, with numerous villages affected, along with the region of Bhutni. Erosion from the flooding, reported from Khaskol, led to a disruption in river flow which led to a more severe impact in Bhutni. More than 100 boats have been sent out for evacuation. At East Basudevpur, a 20ft (6-metre) embankment collapsed, reducing the channel from 550ft to under 150ft, which could lead to further flooding unless repaired. This flooding resulted after the Ganges River rose about 75cm above its “extreme danger” level owing to heavy rainfall. View image in fullscreen Houses partially submerged by flood waters from the Ganges River in Patna earlier this month. Photograph: Sachin Kumar/AFP/Getty Images A swell caused by Hurricane Marie led to significant beach erosion across Orange county in California on 7 September. The erosion formed a cliff edge on some of the beaches, along with exposing old asphalt, pipes and even pieces of an old pier. The flooding caused by the swell damaged homes and vehicles, as well as flooding streets, leaving behind a layer of sand. The swell has been estimated to be between 8 and 10ft tall. Local people say it is not uncommon to see beach erosion, but this has been one of the most severe cases. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Down to Earth The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential after newsletter promotion After the hottest summer on record for the US , the above average temperatures are expected to continue this week as a heatwave grips many central states. A persistent area of high pressure and a very warm surface after recent heat will help to drive the daytime temperatures widely into the high 30s celsius or up to 40C across Oklahoma, Kansas and nearby states. Models keep the heat locked in through much of the remainder of the month, increasing the risk of wildfires, with other parts of the country already under red flag warnings. World NGO Day is a day of global awareness and celebration of non-governmental organizations (NGOs) and nonprofits, and the humanitarian work they do, held every year on February 27. Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Merridee Book, CEO and Artistic Director of the Coronado Island Film Festival, recently also became an Executive Advisor on the World NGO Day Global Council. World NGO Day is a day of global awareness and celebration of non-governmental organizations (NGOs) and nonprofits, and the humanitarian work they do, held every year on February 27. Book had previously met with Marcis Skadmanis, the Latvian founder of World NGO Day, to discuss collaborations around the event. “He invited me to be an executive director, which is quite an honor,” Book said. “When I started looking at what they were doing, and they were reaching out for more executive advisors, the parallel between what I’ve done professionally throughout my career and with the film festival for the past decade or so – it’s all about storytelling. It’s a day that recognizes everyone.” She explained some of the history behind the event, which was first officially recognized in 2010 by the Baltic Sea Forum and has since gained traction and support on a global scale from entities like the United Nations, European Union, and countries across continents. “The team is very international, which is one of the things that really appealed to me,” Book said. “Whenever I’m watching documentaries that are highlighting some amazing people across the globe, I always get excited to share those at our film festival. Often, people wouldn’t know about this individual (why or how would we?), but through the power of visual storytelling and cinema, we get to introduce them to that person who is changing lives across the world. And maybe it inspires someone here to do something similar.” On that note, Book added that those stories are the core of what makes the issues these organizations are tackling connect with people on a human level and in a way that may inspire action. “That’s one of the reasons I’ve always been drawn to cinema. Statistics can be powerful when they’re shared in a way that people can quantify them, but it’s the personal stories that move us. And I’ve been involved with nonprofits in varying capacities my whole life, so this was kind of an easy transition into representing the [World NGO Day] platform in a bigger, more profound way. You’re celebrating inspiration, and you’re also shifting public understanding [of issues and solutions].” Book noted that having a day specifically to celebrate NGOs and nonprofits allows for organizations to create a coordinated effort in shining the light on their efforts. “It makes people pause and reflect on the work that a lot of people are doing very quietly,” she explained. “They’re often doing this work under the radar and at local levels across the globe, and that work is driven by people who are passionate about a cause and action-oriented.” In fact, one partner that the World NGO Day organization works closely with is the United Nations (UN). “The UN put together the UN Millennium Development Goals. Back in 2000, there were eight global targets the UN member states decided that they would focus on for the next 15 years, that included reducing poverty, hunger, disease, gender inequality, lack of education, and clean water. These are big global issues that transcend all of our societies and transcend borders, whether it’s first world or third world nations,” Book mentioned. She added that while major strides were made by 2015, with things like extreme poverty being cut in half and millions of lives saved from deadly diseases, progress wasn’t always applied evenly across the world, and there’s still a lot of work to be done. A post-2015 plan evolved from the Millennium Development Goals, the Sustainable Development Plan, which now provides a plan with a more cohesive scope and level of clarity that aligns with many of the groups that World NGO Day was created to highlight. “I think it goes to that analogy that one organization out there might not be noticed, but collectively, when there’s an entire day and reason to celebrate something, it’s that united power of voices that people will recognize,” Book commented. “You might not have realized all of the organizations that exist locally are in your region, and through this day of recognition those organizations can potentially find new people who will want to get involved and be a part of that work. “And for me, the attraction to being a part of this group is, ‘How can I further this mission and help guide it,’” Book added. Something she would like to work towards at a local level is seeing World NGO Day thrive across San Diego, suggesting that could be through official ceremonies, awards, and recognition programs to elevate and honor individuals who are making a difference in their communities. She would also like to explore potential programming avenues that could be done at various scales, such as panels with nonprofit leaders, meetups to foster membership or partnerships between groups with connected missions, interviews or fireside chats, and more. Again, things that put the spotlight on the human stories around these important issues. “It’s a win-win for everybody. I’d love to see proclamations and each city celebrate this in their own, unique way, and powerfully bring together and recognize people here in San Diego,” she mentioned. “We live in such an incredible county with so much going on. Between the popping culinary scene, San Diego’s indigenous groups and history, the ocean and ecology, we’ve got the research scene, we’re a border city…there’s just so much that is happening in this county that is unique. “And there are a lot of amazing people doing amazing work through nonprofit organizations here that are impacting people’s lives,” Book noted. “There are some that are tackling poverty and homelessness, some are focused on education, and so on. [World NGO Day] can be the perfect way to shine a light on that and I think my role is engaging with that on a leadership level with organizations and individuals who have the power to amplify this celebration, as well as the local nonprofits who can then utilize this day.” Book is especially excited about the tools that have been made available for free for NGOs and nonprofits through World NGO Day. Toolkits can be found on the World NGO Day website for NGOs and nonprofits, governments, and corporate organizations, with ways to engage communities around local efforts and help nonprofits showcase their missions and impact to the public. Those tools can be found at https://worldngoday.org/celebrate/ . “That’s a big goal of this movement, helping these groups get visibility and more support by leveraging this day to create something that puts the spotlight back on their efforts,” Book said. “It sort of gives you permission to promote your cause in a way that doesn’t feel self-serving and instead feels mission-driven. There’s something like 10 million nonprofits across the world; it’s an extraordinary number. And it’s about bringing that home, bringing it to our own communities.” To learn more about World NGO Day, visit their website at https://worldngoday.org/ . https://www.thetablet.co.uk/news/budapes.text: Budapest archdiocese warns priest off politics after PM’s complaint Alexander Faludy 04 October 2026, The Tablet Prev Next Fr Osztie preaching at the pilgrimage Mass in Feldebrő on 26 September Belvárosi Plébániatemplom / Facebook Fr Zoltán Osztie described Tisza, the centre-right party Péter Magyar leads, as an ‘unbelieving, immoral, traitorous element that betrays the country to the great powers and financial circles’. The Archdiocese of Esztergom-Budapest warned a priest against political interventions after the Hungarian prime minister’s public call for the hierarchy to distance itself from his statements. “I expect the Catholic Church immediately, publicly and completely to condemn the statements made by Zoltán Osztie,” Prime Minister Péter Magyar wrote on social media on Thursday, referring to a sermon preached by Fr Osztie in north-east Hungary the previous Saturday. Fr Osztie was preaching at St Martin’s Church in Feldebrő to a pilgrimage group from his inner-city Budapest parish of Our Lady, which subsequently shared the video on its online channels. Magyar’s social media post included the recording of the sermon, in which Osztie asked: “How many of our Christian brothers and sisters go to church, vote for Tisza, and understand nothing ?” The priest described Tisza, the centre-right party Magyar leads, as an “unbelieving, immoral, traitorous element that betrays the country to the great powers and financial circles”. He told his parishioners: “I am proud, by the way, that there are no such people around me – and if there were, I would wish they weren’t.” Osztie has long been associated with the right-wing populist Fidesz-KDNP alliance led by former prime minister Viktor Orbán, which governed Hungary from 2010 until Magyar’s victory in elections this April . The priest has continued to court controversy since the change of government, celebrating a mass for Orbán’s birthday in May and speaking at a Fidesz organised rally in July. On 20 July he told the left-wing daily Népszava that Magyar was “an instrument of Satan”. Magyar’s post had attracted 55,000 likes and 14,000 comments by Sunday. An early comment came from the official account of the Hungarian Catholic Bishops’ Conference, referring to the bishops’ official statement of neutrality ahead of April 2026 elections. The Archdiocese of Esztergom-Budapest on Friday in its own social media post, saying it was “saddened and shocked to learn of the statements made by Zoltán Osztie during his Mass in Feldebrő”. It continued: “The offensive characterisation and stigmatisation of people are incompatible with the teachings of Christ and do not speak in the spirit of the Gospel.” The archdiocesan office had, the message concluded, “warned and called upon Fr Zoltán Osztie … to remove this video from the parish’s online platforms and to refrain from such and similar statements”.
